bullets: Macbeth’s first line, ‘So foul and fair a day I have not seen’, unknowingly **echoes** the Witches’ ‘Fair is foul’ (1.1): he is linked to them before they meet.
Banquo notices Macbeth ‘start’ and ‘seem to fear / Things that do sound so fair’: fear suggests the idea of murder is already in his mind.

Banquo’s warning: ‘oftentimes, to win us to our harm, / The instruments of darkness tell us truths, / Win us with honest trifles, to betray’s / In deepest consequence.’ He is the **foil** who resists.

Macbeth’s aside: ‘Why do I yield to that suggestion / Whose horrid image doth unfix my hair / And make my seated heart knock at my ribs’: physical horror at his own thought; **personification** of his heart.
‘Present fears / Are less than horrible imaginings’ and ‘My thought, whose murder yet is but fantastical’: the first use of ‘murder’ comes from Macbeth, not the Witches.
‘If chance will have me king, why, chance may crown me / Without my stir’: he briefly considers leaving it to fate.

callouts.p: The Witches never tell Macbeth to kill. The extract proves that the idea of murder comes from him: ideal for questions on ambition, fate and free will, or the supernatural.

core.p: Returning from battle, Macbeth and Banquo meet the Witches on the heath. They hail Macbeth as Thane of Glamis, Thane of Cawdor and ‘king hereafter’, and tell Banquo he will father kings. Ross arrives: Macbeth is now Thane of Cawdor. Macbeth, in **asides**, imagines murder.

bullets: The letter calls her ‘my dearest partner of greatness’: an equal partnership, unusual for the period.
‘Yet do I fear thy nature; / It is too full o’ th’ milk of human kindness / To catch the nearest way’: **milk** = nurture, femininity, gentleness; she sees kindness as weakness.
‘The raven himself is hoarse / That croaks the fatal entrance of Duncan / Under my battlements’: the raven is an **omen** of death; ‘my battlements’ shows her ownership and power.

‘Come, you spirits / That tend on mortal thoughts, unsex me here, / And fill me from the crown to the toe top-full / Of direst cruelty!’: **imperatives** and an invocation that sounds like a witch’s spell; she rejects her gender.
‘Come to my woman’s breasts, / And take my milk for gall’: grotesque image reversing motherhood (gall = bitter bile).
‘Come, thick night, / And pall thee in the dunnest smoke of hell’: darkness imagery to hide the deed from heaven.

‘look like th’ innocent flower, / But be the serpent under’t’: **appearance vs reality**, an allusion to the serpent in Eden, and to the medal struck after the Gunpowder Plot that showed a snake among flowers.

callouts.p: A Jacobean audience believed witches made pacts with spirits. Lady Macbeth’s ‘Come, you spirits’ would sound like witchcraft, which James I wrote about in Daemonologie (1597).

core.p: Lady Macbeth reads Macbeth’s letter, fears his nature, and calls on evil spirits to fill her with cruelty. Macbeth arrives; she plans Duncan’s murder that night.

bullets: ‘If it were done when ’tis done, then ’twere well / It were done quickly’: **repetition** of ‘done’ shows his mind circling; the conditional shows hesitation.
‘He’s here in double trust’: kinsman and host, plus Duncan is his king. Killing him breaks **every bond**.
‘his virtues / Will plead like angels, trumpet-tongued’: religious imagery of judgement; Duncan as a holy king (divine right).

‘I have no spur / To prick the sides of my intent, but only / Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself / And falls on th’ other’: **extended metaphor** of a horse-rider jumping too far: he knows ambition will destroy him.
‘We will proceed no further in this business’: a **firm decision**, euphemistic ‘business’.
Lady Macbeth: ‘Was the hope drunk / Wherein you dressed yourself?’: **clothing** imagery; ridicule.
‘When you durst do it, then you were a man’: she defines masculinity as daring violence.

‘I have given suck… / Have plucked my nipple from his boneless gums / And dashed the brains out, had I so sworn as you / Have done to this’: shocking **infanticide** image; she would break the most natural bond to keep a promise.
‘We fail? / But screw your courage to the sticking-place, / And we’ll not fail.’: practical, commanding; the metaphor of a crossbow string or a peg tightened.
Macbeth: ‘False face must hide what the false heart doth know.’: closing **rhyming couplet**; he adopts her philosophy of deception.

callouts.p: Scene 7 is the first major turning point. Macbeth decides not to kill, then reverses within 50 lines: Lady Macbeth’s influence and his own ambition together tip him over.

core.p: Alone during Duncan’s feast, Macbeth argues himself out of the murder in a soliloquy. Lady Macbeth challenges his manhood and gives him a plan; he agrees.

bullets: Name the **dramatic method**: aside, soliloquy, dialogue, stage action.
Track **shifts**: Macbeth’s hesitation → resolution; Lady Macbeth’s invocation → planning.
Use AO2 terminology precisely: imperative, metaphor, antithesis, euphemism, rhyming couplet.

essays.q: Explore how Shakespeare presents Macbeth’s ambition in Act 1 Scene 7.
essays.text:
Shakespeare opens the scene with Macbeth alone, and the soliloquy exposes a mind trying to talk itself out of murder. The conditional ‘If it were done when ’tis done’ and the triple repetition of ‘done’ create a circular rhythm, as if he cannot get past the act itself. He lists the bonds he would break, ‘He’s here in double trust’, and imagines Duncan’s ‘virtues’ pleading ‘like angels, trumpet-tongued’; the religious imagery of the Last Judgement shows that he fully understands the murder as a sin.

Most strikingly, Macbeth names his own flaw. The extended metaphor of ‘Vaulting ambition, which o’erleaps itself / And falls on th’ other’ pictures a rider leaping onto a horse with such force that he falls off the far side. Ambition is presented as the only ‘spur’ he has, and it is self-defeating; the line even breaks off mid-thought, suggesting he stops before completing the image of his own fall. His resolution, ‘We will proceed no further in this business’, is firm, and the euphemism ‘business’ shows him distancing himself from murder.

Yet Shakespeare makes the reversal swift. Lady Macbeth attacks his masculinity with ‘When you durst do it, then you were a man’, and the brutal image of dashing out her baby’s brains shocks him into submission. By the end Macbeth speaks her language, closing the scene with a rhyming couplet, ‘False face must hide what the false heart doth know’. The neat rhyme suggests a decision now fixed, and the repetition of ‘false’ shows that ambition has been reshaped into a commitment to deception.
essays.thesis: Shakespeare presents ambition as a force Macbeth fully understands and almost resists, so that his decision to kill is a conscious choice rather than a fate imposed on him.
